items.stimulus: A public health team models the number of flu cases in one town with $f(x) = 50(2)^x$, where $x$ is the number of weeks since the first reported case. The outbreak in a second town is modeled by $g$, whose graph is the graph of $y = f(x)$ translated 3 units to the right.
items.stem: At $x = 5$, how many times as many cases does $f$ predict as $g$?
items.explanation: A translation 3 units to the right gives $g(x) = f(x - 3) = 50(2)^{x - 3}$. So $f(5) = 50(2)^5 = 1{,}600$ and $g(5) = 50(2)^2 = 200$. Then $1{,}600 \div 200 = 8$, so $f$ predicts 8 times as many cases.

A.why: You moved the graph the wrong way and used $f(x + 3)$, which shifts it left. That makes $g(5) = 50(2)^8 = 12{,}800$ and the ratio $\frac{1}{8}$. A shift to the right replaces $x$ with $x - 3$.

B.why: You used the shift amount as the ratio. Because each week doubles the count, a 3-week lag makes the values differ by a factor of $2^3 = 8$, not 3.

D.why: 200 is $g(5)$, the number of cases in the second town. The question asks how many times as large $f(5)$ is than that.
